newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb opposition rejects provisional rule, new vote.
newsitem.headline: Serb opposition rejects provisional rule, new vote.

text.p: A Serbian opposition leader on Wednesday rejected a possible government plan to defuse street protests over annulled municipal elections by imposing provisional rule and then holding a new vote.

The opposition Zajedno bloc has staged nine weeks of mass demonstrations in a bid to restore the outcome of November municipal elections in 14 major towns where it claims to have won, a stand endorsed later by OSCE factfinders.

The decision by President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist Party to nullify the vote over murky "irregularities" has withstood legal challenges aside from four towns where Zajedno victories were later verified by Justice Ministry inquiries.

Sources in Milosevic's leftist coalition said this week one option drawn up to overcome the crisis was to institute provisional rule in the capital Belgrade, and possibly other disputed cities, for two months and then call fresh elections.

"This is just unacceptable. It would mean we accept the theft of the November 17 elections and reject OSCE findings," Djindjic told a news conference at his Democratic Party (DS) headquarters in central Belgrade.
Outside, thousands of opposition protesters were rallying noisily for the 66th straight day, facing off with riot police maintaining a cordon to prevent street marches.

Djindjic said Milosevic, who has become even more reclusive than usual during the protest crisis and given no firm clue as to how he planned to resolve it, "lacks a clear concept or even overview" of the problem.

"He seems to think that delaying will make the problem disappear by itself, that people will just get tired and the international community will go back to dealing matter of factly with Milosevic like the old days," Djindjic said.
"There are only two clear answers to this crisis -- return the elections to Zajedno, or say (categorically) they will not be returned -- but he refuses to give one (or the other).

Djindjic said Western warnings that federal Yugoslavia -- Serbia and tiny Montenegro -- will be denied vital economic aid unless election results are respected and democratic reforms begun had apparently not impressed Milosevic yet.
"Any stronger international support for Zajedno we would not want because that would be interference in our internal affairs," Djindjic said.

"unless the election results are honoured he (Milosevic) cannot count on economic or diplomatic cooperation from the (West) that is necessary for any country to survive. And we have very big economic problems."
Djindjic acknowledged that the failure of traditionally pro-Socialist workers to join Zajedno's campaign in any significant number had limited the impact of protests.
But he said it was not realistic to expect many workers to strike when only 25 percent were regularly employed and feared for their jobs.

Zajedno had decided to expand its daily action from the usual 3 p.m. rally in central Belgrade to a random series in varying districts of the capital after nightfall to keep the authorities off balance.
Djindjic also planned to tour Serbian provincial towns in coming days to drum up broader support for Zajedno.
